# Holographic Computer-Generated Holography (CGH) Calculation

Also called: CGH Generation, Hologram Synthesis, Computer-Generated Holography

## Overview
Holographic Computer-Generated Holography (CGH) Calculation refers to the computational methods used to synthesize the interference or diffraction patterns (holograms) that reconstruct 3D light fields when displayed on devices such as Spatial Light Modulators (SLMs) or volumetric displays. The primary problem it solves is the translation of discrete 3D scene data (voxels, point clouds, or meshes) into a 2D complex amplitude or phase-only pattern that, when illuminated, produces the desired 3D optical reconstruction. What sets this family apart from sibling methods like [Galvanometer Scanner Volume Rendering](5277-galvanometer-scanner-volume-rendering.md) or [Multi-view Lenticular Volume Rendering](6636-multi-view-lenticular-volume-rendering.md) is that CGH methods explicitly simulate wave optics (interference and diffraction) to encode depth and parallax information directly into the phase or amplitude of light, rather than relying on geometric projection or time-multiplexed scanning.

## Shared principles
All methods in this family share the fundamental goal of generating a 2D complex field $U(x,y)$ or a phase-only map $\phi(x,y)$ that serves as the input to a display device. The core mathematical principle governing the relationship between the object plane (the 3D scene) and the hologram plane is wave propagation. This is typically modeled using scalar diffraction theory, most commonly the Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) or the Fresnel approximation.

The general forward propagation from an object point at position $\mathbf{r}_0 = (x_0, y_0, z_0)$ to a point $\mathbf{r} = (x, y, z)$ on the hologram plane is described by the spherical wave solution to the Helmholtz equation:
$$ U(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{A}{|\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0|} \exp\left(i k |\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0|\right) $$
where $A$ is the amplitude (often derived from the object's intensity or color) and $k = 2\pi/\lambda$ is the wavenumber. The total hologram field is the superposition of contributions from all object points:
$$ U_{total}(x,y) = \sum_{j} U_j(x,y) $$

For phase-only SLMs, the complex field must be encoded into a phase pattern $\phi_h(x,y)$, often using algorithms like Gerchberg-Saxton or direct phase quantization, where the amplitude is discarded or normalized. The computational bottleneck for all methods is the $O(N^2 \log N)$ or $O(N^3)$ complexity of calculating these interactions for high-resolution holograms, leading to various optimization strategies such as subsampling, look-up tables, or iterative optimization.

## Subtopics

### [Volume Rendering based CGH Calculation](808-volume-rendering-based-cgh-calculation.md)
This method treats volumetric data (voxels) as transparent objects with diffuse reflection properties. It differs from direct point-source summation by simulating light attenuation and Lambertian reflection, allowing for the reconstruction of transparent and multi-layer objects with depth cues. It is computationally expensive but preserves transparency better than Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) methods. An approximate variant reduces cost by dividing the hologram into elemental holograms and calculating light propagation only once per elemental hologram using its center pixel.

### [Diffraction-Specific Approach](7015-diffraction-specific-approach.md)
Also known as the Hogel Vector Approach, this method bypasses direct optical interference simulation. It treats the hologram as a collection of subsampled functional elements ("hogels") represented spectrally as "hogel vectors". It works backwards from the 3D image, rendering orthographic projections to generate data, and decoding them using precomputed basis fringes. It sets itself apart by explicitly utilizing spatial and spectral subsampling to achieve significant bandwidth compression and computation speedups, at the cost of added image blur.

### [Holographic Stereogram](7067-holographic-stereogram.md)
A Holographic Stereogram generates a hologram from a series of discrete 2D perspective views of an object scene. It produces a view-dependent image that presents the corresponding perspective view in each horizontally displaced direction, functioning similarly to lenticular displays. Unlike full-parallax methods that compute complex interference patterns for all viewing angles, this method approximates the holographic fringe by combining these discrete views, allowing for computation at nearly interactive rates on specialized hardware.

### [Computational Phase Modulation (CGH Generation)](7284-computational-phase-modulation-cgh-generation.md)
This method generates a phase-only CGH displayed on an SLM to reconstruct a target 3D intensity distribution $I_r$ using iterative optimization. It differs from direct phase quantization by actively optimizing the phase pattern to achieve uniform intensity across multiple focal spots or complex volumetric shapes, rather than simply encoding the argument of the complex field. It is distinct from [Volume Rendering based CGH Calculation](808-volume-rendering-based-cgh-calculation.md) which typically relies on superposition of point sources without iterative feedback.

### [Inverse Design Algorithm for Voxel-based CGVHs](8543-inverse-design-algorithm-for-voxel-based-cgvhs.md)
This algorithm designs 3D refractive index structures (voxels) that convert $N$ mutually incoherent transverse input modes $\{u_n\}$ into $N$ target modes $\{v_n\}$ with a one-to-one mapping. It solves the problem of optimizing discrete voxel distributions in a finite volume to maximize mode conversion efficiency. It differs from direct superposition methods by using an iterative forward-backward propagation scheme to locally optimize voxel choices based on overlap integrals, rather than calculating holograms from first principles for each point source.

### [Multiple Wavefront Recording Planes (WRP) with Horizontal Parallax Only (HPO)](10810-multiple-wavefront-recording-planes-wrp-with-horizontal-para.md)
This method generates horizontal parallax only (HPO) CGHs from point clouds by distributing computation across multiple parallel wavefront recording planes (WRPs). It solves the computational bottleneck of direct point-cloud holography by using pre-computed look-up tables (LUTs) for propagation between these planes, while adapting the geometry to compute 1D hololines instead of full 2D holograms. It is distinguished from full-parallax WRP methods by its reduction of the diffraction calculation to a single horizontal dimension per plane.

### Ray-tracing Method for Full-Parallax CGHs
- **Definition**: Calculates computer-generated holograms by simulating ray paths to remove hidden surfaces and render realistic material properties [S1, unofficial].
- **Steps**: Cast rays from every elementary hologram into virtual objects. Determine the traveling paths of the rays. Consider intersection with objects, absorption, reflection, and refraction during path calculation. Express multiple reflections and refractions by casting additional rays into the reflection and transmission directions. Calculate the length of the light path for each ray. Apply the Phong reflection model and Cook–Torrance reflection model to express material quality [S1, unofficial].
- **Pitfall**: Hidden surfaces must be explicitly removed to avoid incorrect holographic fringe generation [S1, unofficial].

### Multiple Reference Plane (MRP) approach
- **Definition**: Reduces reconstruction error and blur in holographic stereograms by assigning reference planes to different depth segments of a 3D scene [S1, unofficial].
- **Steps**: Divide the 3D scene into several parts along its depth direction. Set a reference plane for each of the object parts. Resynthesize all effectively synthetic perspective images referred to their own reference planes of the object parts. Generate the finally effectively synthetic perspective image exposed to one holographic elemental by only once exposure [S1, unofficial].
- **Pitfall**: Traditional EPISM causes distortion and blur for object points located far away from the reference plane [S1, unofficial].

### Holographic Defuser Light Field Display
- **Definition**: A system combining a rotating holographic defuser and a high-speed projector to form multiple viewpoints in 360 degrees. The holographic defuser reflects images within a limited range of 1.25 degrees, updating the image synchronized with rotation to generate viewpoints [S2, unofficial].
- **Parameter**: Reflection angle range: 1.25 degrees [S2, unofficial].

### Color Holovideo via Additive Primaries
- **Definition**: Production of full-color holographic images by computing three separate fringes for additive primary colors (red, green, blue) accounting for different wavelengths, and modulating three separate laser beams [S3].
- **Steps**: 1. Compute three separate fringes, one for each additive primary color (red, green, blue), considering their specific wavelengths. 2. Use each fringe to modulate a separate beam of light corresponding to that primary color [S3].

### Off-axis interferometry for complex field retrieval
- **Definition**: A technique to measure the complex light field (amplitude and phase) at the output facet of a CGVH by interfering the signal with a tilted reference wave, allowing characterization of mode sorting quality [S4, unofficial].
- **Steps**: Tilt the reference wave such that interference fringes have a period of about 3 pixels. Capture the intensity image (interferogram). Compute the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) of the intensity image. Crop a 60x60 pixel region around one sideband in the frequency domain. Compute the inverse FFT of the cropped sideband to obtain the complex field. Apply corrections using a Nelder-Mead optimizer to maximize the overlap integral between the measured field (at 0° AOI) and the target mode (e.g., HG1,1). The seven optimized parameters are then used to correct all experimentally recorded fields [S4, unofficial].
- **Pitfall**: The retrieved field may show poor overlap with target modes due to: 1) imperfect centering on the pixel grid, 2) small geometric rotation in experimental images, 3) global phase tilt and defocus, and 4) slight differences in mode waist compared to simulation [S4, unofficial].

### Rendering Framework for Autostereoscopic Displays
- **Steps**: The framework consists of four sequential pre-processing steps applied to the hologram to acquire a set of reconstruction images corresponding to views from a camera rotating around the scene. The resolution of these images equals the 2D resolution of the screen [S5]. Step 1: View extraction. Step 2: Suppression of aperture diffraction (apodization). Step 3: Back propagation. Step 4: Colour balancing [S5].
- **Complexity**: The computational complexity of the framework is $O(NM)$. The back propagation requires only 1D FFTs with a pre-computed kernel due to the same distance [S5].
- **Number**: Performance test on a 3.3 GHz Intel Core i7-5820 CPU with Windows 8 (x64). For the 'Dice' dataset (142,903 points), processing times per view were: View extraction 0.04s, Apodization 0.38s, Back propagation 16.33s, Colour balancing 1.19s [S5]. Rendering on an Holografika HoloVizio 722RC light field display (72 projectors, 70° viewing angle). 70 views were extracted with an angular resolution of 1° and a 2D resolution of 1280x768 pixels [S5].

### Back Propagation
- **Steps**: The apodized aperture is zero-padded to the size of the full hologram to represent the hologram from that specific viewing position. It is then back-propagated using BL-ASM to reconstruct the hologram for the corresponding view [S5]. To visualize the reconstructed object, the magnitude (square root of the intensity) of the complex wavefield computed by the back propagation is extracted. This magnitude matches the gamma curves for displays and is stored as a 2D image [S5].

## Background
The concept of Computer-Generated Holography (CGH) originated from the work of Emmett N. Leith and Juris Upatnieks in 1962, who described the process from a communication-theory viewpoint, showing that hologram construction involves modulation operations [S1, unofficial]. Early CGH focused on point-source models. The field has since expanded to include volume rendering techniques for volumetric displays [S1, unofficial], ray-tracing for realistic material rendering [S1, unofficial], and iterative phase modulation for SLM-based displays [S1, unofficial][S3]. Recent developments include inverse design algorithms for voxel-based computer-generated volume holograms (CGVHs) in glass [S4, unofficial] and methods for autostereoscopic light field displays [S5]. The integration of CGH with volumetric displays aims to provide true 3D visualization without the need for head-mounted displays or glasses [S2, unofficial].
